issues.legal_issue: Land factually included as a single entry in a register prepared and maintained under the applicable land-registration law qualifies as an estate under the abolition statute even if its entry may have been improper under that law.
material_facts: The land was held by its proprietor, who therefore fell within the relevant definition of an intermediary if the land was an estate.
The land was undisputedly included under one entry in a general register of revenue-paying lands.
The register was one of the registers prepared and maintained under the applicable land-registration law.
The proprietor argued that the land did not meet the separate definition of an estate under the land-registration law and therefore could not validly have been entered in the register.
issues.conclusion: The land qualified as an estate because it was factually included under one entry in the specified register; whether it was properly or validly entered was irrelevant to the definition applied.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(g) and 3(1) of the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, land held by an intermediary and included under one entry in a general register prepared and maintained under the law for the time being in force is an estate. Sections 4, 7 and 20 of the Bengal Land Registration Act, 1876, identified the relevant registers. The statutory reference to the register identifies where the land was included; it does not require that the entry be valid or proper under the separate definition of estate in the registration law. The court distinguished Biswambhar Singh v. State of Orissa, which concerned a different part of the definition of intermediary.

predicates.land_status_determination_under_abolitio: The proceeding requires a determination whether land falls within a statutory definition of an estate for abolition purposes.
predicates.land_listed_as_single_entry_in_specified: The land is factually included under one entry in a general register prepared and maintained under the applicable law.

issues.definition: When a proceeding requires an estate-status determination, land held by an intermediary and factually listed as a single entry in the specified register qualifies as an estate.

issues.legal_issue: A respondent in an appeal is not barred from relying on a ground merely because it was omitted from the respondent’s statement of case.
material_facts: The proceeding was an appeal in which the respondent relied on estoppel although the ground was not included in its statement of case.
The estoppel plea had been raised and made an issue in the High Court, where it was elaborately addressed.
The appellant could not claim surprise from the respondent’s reliance on the plea.
issues.conclusion: The court declined to exclude the respondent’s estoppel plea because the rules imposed no corresponding restriction on a respondent and there was no surprise in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Order XIX, rule 4 of the Supreme Court Rules restricts an appellant from relying, without leave, on grounds omitted from the appellant’s statement of case; there is no corresponding rule imposing that disability on a respondent. The court also observed that it may, in an appropriate case, permit an appellant to raise an omitted ground. The principle concerning the appellant’s restriction was consistent with Sheo Singh Rai v. Mussumut Dakho. Here, because the plea had been litigated below and caused no surprise, it was not shut out.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and respondent_relies_on_omitted_ground and ground_was_litigated_below and no_surprise_to_opposing_party

predicates.respondent_relies_on_omitted_ground: The respondent relies on a ground that was omitted from its statement of case.
predicates.ground_was_litigated_below: The ground was raised and considered in the court below.
predicates.no_surprise_to_opposing_party: The opposing party is not taken by surprise by the ground.

issues.definition: In an appeal, a respondent may rely on an omitted ground when it was litigated below and does not surprise the opposing party.

issues.legal_issue: A consent decree can estop a party and its successor from relitigating a foundational issue that the decree resolved between the parties.
material_facts: In an earlier suit, the predecessor in title claimed rights over river beds by relying on a asserted sovereign status and the rights said to follow from that status.
The status underlying that claim was directly and substantially in issue in the earlier litigation and was understood by the parties to be central to it.

The parties settled the appeal by consent decree, whose terms recognized the claimant as proprietor of a permanently settled estate and treated the relevant rights as rights of an estate holder rather than of a sovereign ruler.
The current claimant, as successor in title, sought to deny that the land was an estate and thereby assert a status inconsistent with the compromise decree.
issues.conclusion: The consent decree estopped the claimant from reasserting the status and title inconsistent with the decree.
issues.legal_principle: A judgment by consent is as effective in creating an estoppel between the parties as a judgment after contest. The test is whether the prior judgment could have been passed without determination of the issue raised in the later proceeding. The court relied on In re South American and Mexican Company, Ex parte Bank of England; Kinch v. Walcott; Secretary of State for India in Council v. Ateendranath Das; Bhaishanker Nanabhai v. Morarji Keshavji and Co.; and Raja Kumara Venkata Perumal Raja Bahadur v. Thatha Ramasamy Chetty. A successor in title could not reopen the foundational status issue resolved by the compromise decree.

predicates.current_proceeding_reopens_prior_status_: The proceeding seeks to relitigate a status issue that was addressed in an earlier case.
predicates.prior_case_between_related_parties: The earlier case involved the same parties or persons whose interests are represented by their successors in title.
predicates.prior_issue_was_foundational: The status issue was central to the earlier claim and was directly and substantially in issue.
predicates.consent_decree_recognized_inconsistent_s: The earlier case ended in a consent decree whose terms recognized a status inconsistent with the position later asserted.

issues.definition: A party or successor cannot reassert a status in a later proceeding when a consent decree in a related earlier case resolved that foundational status issue inconsistently.

issues.legal_issue: A party may be estopped by a compromise representation about its status when the opposing party gave reciprocal concessions on the basis of that representation.
material_facts: The predecessor in title agreed in the compromise that the property was a permanently settled estate and accepted rights in that capacity rather than asserting sovereign status.
The opposing party gave up the benefit of a judgment in its favour and agreed not to levy further assessment on specified future accretions.
The compromise terms showed that the parties’ concessions were reciprocal and that the estate-status admission was a material basis for the settlement.
The successor later asserted a position inconsistent with the predecessor’s representation.
issues.conclusion: The compromise also estopped the claimant by representation from denying the estate-holder status accepted in the settlement.
issues.legal_principle: A compromise may operate as a representation where one party makes an admission about its status and the other party gives concessions on the basis of that admission. The court found from the terms of the compromise that the concessions were reciprocal, that the estate-status admission was a main consideration, and that no further evidence was needed to establish that basis.

predicates.current_proceeding_denies_prior_represen: The proceeding asserts a position inconsistent with a status previously accepted in a compromise.
predicates.compromise_representation_by_predecessor: A predecessor in interest represented in a compromise that the property was held in a particular status.
predicates.opposing_party_made_reciprocal_concessio: The opposing party gave reciprocal concessions on the basis of that representation.

issues.definition: A party cannot deny a status represented by its predecessor in a compromise when the opposing party made reciprocal concessions in reliance on it.
